stimulus.title: Humanities: Music for Silent Pictures
stimulus.text:
The phrase “silent film” has always been something of a misnomer. In the decades before synchronized sound arrived in the late 1920s, almost no one watched a movie in silence. In large city theaters, orchestras of thirty or more musicians played elaborate scores. In small-town movie houses, a single pianist or organist sat below the screen, often playing for several hours a day, six or seven days a week. The pictures were silent; the experience of seeing them was anything but.

What these musicians did is difficult to reconstruct, because much of it was never written down. Studios sometimes distributed cue sheets suggesting appropriate pieces for each scene, such as a lively march for a parade or something mournful for a deathbed, and publishers sold thick anthologies of short, adaptable pieces sorted by mood. But many accompanists, especially in smaller theaters, improvised. They watched the screen and made up music to fit it, shifting key and tempo as a chase gave way to a love scene or a storm broke over a ship at sea. A good accompanist could make an audience laugh at a pratfall a split second before it happened, or hold a room perfectly still.

The work demanded an unusual combination of skills. An accompanist needed a large repertoire, a quick ear, and the stamina to play through a whole program without a break. Above all, he or she needed to watch the film as closely as any audience member while performing for that audience at the same time. Accompanists spoke of “catching” a film, as if it were something moving that had to be met at exactly the right moment. A beat too late, and a joke fell flat; a mood held too long, and a tragedy turned comic.

When synchronized sound arrived, these musicians lost their jobs with remarkable speed. Within a few years, thousands of theater musicians across the country were out of work, replaced by recorded soundtracks that were identical at every showing. Some found work in radio or in the new sound studios, but they were the fortunate few. Musicians' unions protested, sometimes with newspaper advertisements warning audiences that “canned music” would make films colder and cheaper. The public, delighted by the novelty of hearing actors speak, largely did not listen.

It would be easy to tell this story as a simple loss, and in many ways it was one. But it is worth noticing what was gained along with what disappeared. A recorded score allowed filmmakers to control exactly what audiences heard, so that a film in a small town sounded the same as a film in a grand theater. Composers could write music shaped to every second of a scene, knowing it would be played precisely the same way each time. Much of the film music that audiences now admire depends on that precision.

What disappeared was something harder to name: the sense that each showing was a live event, shaped in part by the person at the piano and by the room itself. An accompanist could respond to a particular audience, stretching a gag that was getting big laughs or hurrying through a scene that had the crowd restless. No two screenings were quite the same. Musicians who played the same film all week often said that no two audiences laughed in exactly the same places. The film was fixed; the performance around it was not.

In recent decades, that older experience has enjoyed a modest revival. Film festivals and archives now present restored silent films with live musicians, some playing historical scores and others improvising in the old way. Audiences who attend these screenings often describe being surprised by how alive the films feel. The surprise is itself revealing. We have grown so used to films that are identical every time that we have forgotten they were once something closer to a concert: a collaboration, renewed every night, between the screen and the people in front of it.

stimulus.title: Humanities: Music for Silent Pictures
stimulus.text:
The phrase “silent film” has always been something of a misnomer. In the decades before synchronized sound arrived in the late 1920s, almost no one watched a movie in silence. In large city theaters, orchestras of thirty or more musicians played elaborate scores. In small-town movie houses, a single pianist or organist sat below the screen, often playing for several hours a day, six or seven days a week. The pictures were silent; the experience of seeing them was anything but.

What these musicians did is difficult to reconstruct, because much of it was never written down. Studios sometimes distributed cue sheets suggesting appropriate pieces for each scene, such as a lively march for a parade or something mournful for a deathbed, and publishers sold thick anthologies of short, adaptable pieces sorted by mood. But many accompanists, especially in smaller theaters, improvised. They watched the screen and made up music to fit it, shifting key and tempo as a chase gave way to a love scene or a storm broke over a ship at sea. A good accompanist could make an audience laugh at a pratfall a split second before it happened, or hold a room perfectly still.

The work demanded an unusual combination of skills. An accompanist needed a large repertoire, a quick ear, and the stamina to play through a whole program without a break. Above all, he or she needed to watch the film as closely as any audience member while performing for that audience at the same time. Accompanists spoke of “catching” a film, as if it were something moving that had to be met at exactly the right moment. A beat too late, and a joke fell flat; a mood held too long, and a tragedy turned comic.

When synchronized sound arrived, these musicians lost their jobs with remarkable speed. Within a few years, thousands of theater musicians across the country were out of work, replaced by recorded soundtracks that were identical at every showing. Some found work in radio or in the new sound studios, but they were the fortunate few. Musicians' unions protested, sometimes with newspaper advertisements warning audiences that “canned music” would make films colder and cheaper. The public, delighted by the novelty of hearing actors speak, largely did not listen.

It would be easy to tell this story as a simple loss, and in many ways it was one. But it is worth noticing what was gained along with what disappeared. A recorded score allowed filmmakers to control exactly what audiences heard, so that a film in a small town sounded the same as a film in a grand theater. Composers could write music shaped to every second of a scene, knowing it would be played precisely the same way each time. Much of the film music that audiences now admire depends on that precision.

What disappeared was something harder to name: the sense that each showing was a live event, shaped in part by the person at the piano and by the room itself. An accompanist could respond to a particular audience, stretching a gag that was getting big laughs or hurrying through a scene that had the crowd restless. No two screenings were quite the same. Musicians who played the same film all week often said that no two audiences laughed in exactly the same places. The film was fixed; the performance around it was not.

In recent decades, that older experience has enjoyed a modest revival. Film festivals and archives now present restored silent films with live musicians, some playing historical scores and others improvising in the old way. Audiences who attend these screenings often describe being surprised by how alive the films feel. The surprise is itself revealing. We have grown so used to films that are identical every time that we have forgotten they were once something closer to a concert: a collaboration, renewed every night, between the screen and the people in front of it.
